# A third variable, and more

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

You have more columns than the flat page has positions. Where do the rest go?
`x` and `y` are already taken. A further variable can go in one of four places.
The first is a refining channel: `color`, `size`, `shape`, `pattern` or
`opacity`. The second is the third position, `z`. The third is `play`, which
gives the variable one frame per value, and the fourth is `facet`, which gives
it one panel per value. This chapter uses all four. Each channel answers one
kind of question, and a refining channel gets the legend that decodes it.
When many measurements matter equally, there is a fifth place: `x` itself.
Each value of each measurement becomes a row, and the measurement names become
the categories on `x`.

## Which plot fits which columns?

The recipes in this chapter start from a question. If you start from your table
instead, find the row below that describes your columns, and follow its links:

| Your columns | What to try | Recipes |
|---|---|---|
| Measurements in one unit | three on `x`, `y` and `z` in a cube; four or more as parallel coordinates | [Three measurements](#what-if-three-measurements-matter-equally), [four or more](#what-if-four-or-more-measurements-matter-equally) |
| Measurements in different units | two on `x` and `y`, a third on `size` or `color`; for four or more, standardize each one first | [Size](#how-big-is-each-observation), [color](#what-if-the-third-variable-is-continuous), [four or more](#what-if-four-or-more-measurements-matter-equally) |
| Measurements and categories | a category on `color` or `shape`, or one panel or frame for each of its values | [Color](#which-group-does-each-row-belong-to), [shape](#will-it-read-in-gray), [panels and frames](#what-if-the-structure-needs-three-dimensions) |
| Categories and one measurement | stacked bars in polar, or tiles with the measurement on `color`; a third category into panels | [Storm seasons](#what-if-every-column-is-categorical), [which are alike](#which-categories-are-alike) |
| Categories only | count the rows, with [`count`](../transforms.qmd#count-frequency-aggregation) or in your language first; then as in the row above | [Storm seasons](#what-if-every-column-is-categorical) |

A table often has more columns than one plot can show. Choose the columns that
answer your question, and leave the others out.

## Which group does each row belong to?

The first scatter in [Two variables](two-variables.qmd), GDP per person against
life expectancy, draws every country as an identical dot. Nothing in it says
which continent a country belongs to. The `continent` column is categorical. A
category is carried by `color`, and the palette gives each category one hue:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by
continent."*

**One atom away.** For the same split without hues, swap `color` for `shape`,
and each continent gets its own glyph instead. The `group` channel cannot do
this on a scatter. It splits a mark that joins rows, such as `line`, and a point
joins nothing. See [Channels](../channels.qmd).

## Will it read in gray?

That plot separates the continents by hue alone. Hue works on a screen, but not
in grayscale print, in poor light, or for a colorblind reader. When a plot has
to work in all three of those conditions, bind `color` *and* `shape` to the same
column, so each group is said twice. The `iris_flowers` table has three species
of flower, and here each one gets both its own color and its own glyph:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_flowers)
```

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + point + x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) +
  color(species) + shape(species) +
  palette("okabe")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: points, x is petal length, y is sepal length, color by
species, shape by species, with the okabe palette."*

Printed in gray, *setosa* and *versicolor* become nearly the same shade. Their
glyphs, circles for *setosa* and squares for *versicolor*, still show which
group is which. Saying one column twice is called **redundant encoding**.
`palette()` chooses which colors the `color` channel uses: here the Okabe and
Ito colorblind-safe set. Owning chapters: [Channels](../channels.qmd), [Setting
vs mapping](../style.qmd).

## How big is each observation?

The last two recipes put a category on a channel. This one puts a measurement
there, and it returns to the countries. Population is a third measurement of
each country, and both positions are already taken by GDP per person and life
expectancy. A magnitude is carried by `size`. That channel answers the question
*how much*, so it accepts a continuous column and nothing else:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  size(population)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, size by
population."*

The two largest circles are China and India. A legend decodes the radius.
Owning chapter: [Channels](../channels.qmd).

## What if four variables matter?

The recipes so far bound `color` to the continent and `size` to the population,
one column at a time. You may need both at once, to see which continent a
country is in and how many people live there. Channels compose: any channel a
mark accepts works beside any other channel it accepts. That rule is
[Orthogonality](../design-laws.qmd#law-1-orthogonality). GDP per person, life expectancy,
population and continent in one sentence:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point +
  x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + size(population) +
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by
continent, size by population."*

Every channel keeps its own rule and its own legend; none of them changed
meaning by being combined. Four variables are usually the most a single plot
can carry. Beyond four, use [panels](../faceting.qmd) instead of more channels.

## What if the third variable is continuous?

Now return to three columns. A continuous third column does not have to go on
`size`. Here population goes on `color` instead, so every dot keeps the same
size and the color carries the number. `color` accepts either kind of column. A
continuous column gets a sequential ramp, from light to dark, instead of a
categorical palette. A skewed column reads better on a log ramp. On a linear
ramp, China and India would sit alone at the dark end, and almost every other
country would get the same light shade:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, scale = "log")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by
population on a log scale."*

The legend becomes a labeled ramp. The channel and its rule did not
change; only the kind of column did. [Scales](../scales.qmd) owns the log scale.

## What if three measurements matter equally?

The iris flowers from the grayscale recipe above carry three measurements each,
and none of them is less important than the others. `color` or `size` would make
the third measurement a refinement, and the plot would still be about the other
two. When three *measurements* matter equally, the third one is a position, not
a refinement. Put one measurement on each of `x`, `y` and `z`, and the plot
becomes a cube:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(sepal_length) + y(sepal_width) + z(petal_length) +
  color(species)
```

*"Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is sepal width, z is
petal length, color by species."*

*Setosa* sits apart, near the bottom of the cube, because its petals are short.
*Versicolor* and *virginica* sit higher, and from this side they overlap.

**One atom away.** The viewing angle is a property of the space, not of the
data. `turn` says which side of the cube you look at, and `tilt` says how high
your eye is:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(sepal_length) + y(sepal_width) + z(petal_length) +
  color(species) +
  space(turn = -50, tilt = 15)
```

*"Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is sepal width, z is
petal length, color by species, turned -50, tilted 15."*

From this side *versicolor* and *virginica* overlap less.
[Space](../space.qmd) owns the third dimension.

## What if four or more measurements matter equally?

A cube has room for three measurements. The iris flowers have a fourth, petal
width, and a table can have many more. A **parallel coordinates** plot gives
each measurement a slot of its own on `x`, and draws each flower as one line
through its values.

For that, the table needs one row for each flower and measurement, with the
measurement's name in one column and its value in another. Making that table is
not gog's job: gog never reshapes a table, as [The table has to be
tidy](../data.qmd#the-table-has-to-be-tidy) explains. You make it before you
write the sentence, with the data manipulation tools of the language you are
already using: `tidyr::pivot_longer()` in R, `pandas.melt()` in Python,
`DataFrames.stack()` in Julia, or a short loop in JavaScript.
`iris_measurements` holds the 150 flowers that way, in 600 rows:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_measurements)
```

```{r}
data(iris_measurements) + x(measurement) + y(cm) + color(species) +
  line + group(flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) +
  line * mean + style(size = 3)
```

*"Given the iris measurements: x is measurement, y is cm, color by species,
lines grouped by flower, with opacity 0.2, and also lines derived by mean, with
size 3."*

Each measurement is one slot on `x`, in the order it first appears in the
table. The sentence has two `line` layers. In the first, `group(flower)` splits
the 600 rows into 150 faint lines, and each line joins one flower's four values.
`group(flower)` is written after the first `line`, so it splits that layer
alone. The second layer is `line * mean`. `color(species)` is written before
both marks, so it splits both layers, and in each slot `mean` averages the
flowers of each species. Each species gets one thick line through its four
means, and the faint lines show how far each flower is from its species' line.
[Each country and its continent's mean or
median](../marks/line.qmd#each-country-and-its-continents-mean-or-median) uses
the same two layers.

The three thick lines have three different shapes. *Setosa*'s line is low in
both petal slots, far below the other two species. *Virginica* has the longest
and widest petals, and *versicolor*'s petals are between those of *setosa* and
*virginica*.

**One atom away.** Add `polar()`, and the slots are spread around a circle.
Each flower's line closes into a star. This is the radar chart from
[Line](../marks/line.qmd#a-category-on-the-domain-the-profile), drawn once for
each flower instead of once through the continents' means:

```{r}
data(iris_measurements) + x(measurement) + y(cm) + color(species) +
  line + group(flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) +
  line * mean + style(size = 3) + polar()
```

*"Given the iris measurements: x is measurement, y is cm, color by species,
lines grouped by flower, with opacity 0.2, and also lines derived by mean, with
size 3, in polar."*

The ring marked 0 is a small ring at the center, so each arm grows with the
measurement in centimeters. Sepal length has the largest values, so every star
is longest toward `sepal length`. The three thick stars, one for each species, have three
shapes. *Setosa*'s star has very short petal arms. *Virginica*'s star is the
largest toward every slot except `sepal width`.

All four measurements are in centimeters, so they share the `y` axis as they
are. Every slot shares that one axis. So when the units differ, such as dollars
and years, the measurement with the largest numbers sets the range of the axis,
and the lines of the others look almost flat. In that case, standardize each
measurement before you plot: subtract its mean and divide by its standard
deviation. Every measurement then has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
Like the reshaping, this is a step for the data manipulation tools of your
language, done before you write the sentence. The iris measurements need no
such step, but standardizing them shows something new: 0 becomes the average in
every slot. The `standardized` column holds the result:

```{r}
data(iris_measurements) + x(measurement) + y(standardized) + color(species) +
  line + group(flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) +
  line * mean + style(size = 3)
```

The axis is no longer in centimeters. Its unit is the standard deviation, and 0
in each slot is the mean of that measurement over all 150 flowers. A line above
0 marks a flower larger than average on that measurement. *Setosa*'s thick line
is the only one above 0 in the `sepal width` slot, and it is the lowest in both
petal slots.

## What if the rows form a route?

In the iris cube two sections above, each flower is its own dot, and the order
of the rows means nothing. Sometimes the order is what matters. Here are the two gliders from
[Path](../marks/path.qmd) again. Each row records where one glider was at one
moment, and that glider's next row is two seconds later. So the rows have to be
joined in the order they were recorded. The mark that joins rows in table order
is `path`:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(thermals)
```

```{r}
data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) +
  color(glider) +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal")
```

*"Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by
glider."*

Each route rises because each glider gains altitude. Both gliders start at 900
meters and were recorded for the same 338 seconds. Bravo's first point is drawn
higher than Alpha's, but only because it sits at the back of the cube. In this
view, the back is drawn higher on the page. By the end, Bravo has reached about
2,500 meters and Alpha about 2,100, so Bravo climbs faster.

Nothing in the sentence draws a spiral. The sentence asks `path` to connect the
rows in order. Each glider moves in a circle while it rises, so the connected
rows form a spiral. Look at the crossings as well. At each one the route nearer
to the eye is drawn over the route behind it, and which route is nearer changes
as the two gliders climb. Neither route is drawn entirely in front of the other:
the pieces of both routes are sorted by depth together, as
[Path](../marks/path.qmd#a-path-in-the-cube) explains.

Turn the view, and the same two routes answer a different question. No binding
changes:

```{r}
data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) +
  color(glider) +
  space(turn = 20, tilt = 80) +
  title("The same two routes, seen from overhead")
```

*"Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by
glider, turned 20, tilted 80."*

Seen from nearly overhead the climb is no longer visible, and you are looking
down at two circles, one inside the other. Bravo's circle is half as wide as
Alpha's. Together, the two views show that Bravo climbs faster and turns in a
tighter circle.

These two plots raise one more question. `line`, `step`, `area` and `ribbon`
also join their rows, so why is `path` the only one of the five that takes `z`?
The answer is the difference that separates `path` from `line` on the flat
page: the order in which each one joins its rows. A path joins rows in the
table's order. That order does not depend on any axis, so a third axis does not
change it. A `line` sorts its rows by `x`. In the cube, `x` is one of three
equal positions. At some angles it points straight into the page, and then you
cannot see the order the line was sorted in. That is why a rising route is drawn
with `path`, and why `line` refuses `z` rather than draw a stroke you cannot
read:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(thermals) + line + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) + color(glider)
```

## What if the structure needs three dimensions?

A route is one kind of data that needs three positions, and a physical structure
is another. `quakes_fiji` is the thousand earthquakes from [Map](../map.qmd),
each with a place on the globe and a depth below it. Those three columns,
`east`, `north` and `elevation`, show together what no pair of them shows alone:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(quakes_fiji)
```

```{r}
data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  color(magnitude) + palette("viridis") + space(turn = 120, tilt = 20) +
  title("A thousand earthquakes, and the sheet they lie on")
```

*"Given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, color by
magnitude."*

Color carries a fourth column here, the magnitude of each quake. The vertical
axis is `elevation`, the height above sea level, so a quake 680 km down has the
value −680. That is the deepest quake in the table.

The quakes are not scattered through the cube. They trace a sheet of ocean floor
sinking into the earth. At this angle, east is on the left. The sheet begins
near the surface at the eastern edge and dips west. About a third of the way
from that edge, it is more than 600 km down. The shallower quakes farther west
do not lie on this sheet. They form a separate group. That sheet lies in three
dimensions, so drawing it takes three positions. Any two of them show it
flattened onto the page.

Now cut the quakes into slices of depth and show the slices one after another.
`play(slab)` steps through `slab`, a column that holds the depth in 90 km bands:

```{r}
data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  space(turn = 120, tilt = 20) + play(slab)
```

*"Given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, played by
slab."*

In the web edition the frames play one after another. As they run, the points
move down, and their eastern end moves west. That movement is the slope of the
sheet, read one slice at a time. The frames are not time here. `play` advances
through the levels of an ordered column, and whether that column measures years
or kilometers is a fact about the column, not about `play`. The same atom that
steps through years steps through depths here.

In the PDF, only the first frame is drawn, the slice from 0 to 90 km, and the
panels below replace the motion. They lay the same slices out across the page
instead of showing them one after another in time:

```{r}
data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  space(turn = 120, tilt = 20) | facet(slab, wrap = 4)
```

*"Given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, split into
panel columns by slab, wrapped at 4."*

The eight panels share one set of scales. You compare two depths by looking from
one panel to the next, not by remembering the frame that just played. Whether
you choose panels or frames depends on your readers. Panels let them compare any
two slices, and frames let them see the movement. [Play](../play.qmd) owns that
choice.

## What if every column is categorical?

Every recipe above had at least one measurement. Some tables have none, only
categories. The storms on the globe in [Play](../play.qmd#frames-on-the-globe)
can be described this way. Each storm begins in one month and one hemisphere,
and has one category on the Saffir-Simpson scale of strength, from 1, the
weakest, to 5. Nothing can go on a continuous axis until you count the storms.
The globe's table has a row for every twelve hours of each storm, so gog's
`count` would count those positions, not storms. Making one row per storm and
counting the storms is a step for the data manipulation tools of your language,
like the reshaping for [parallel
coordinates](#what-if-four-or-more-measurements-matter-equally).
`storm_seasons` holds the counts for the 2,174 storms of hurricane strength from
1980 to 2025. Each storm is counted once: in the month and hemisphere where its
track begins, and in the category of its strongest wind. `category` holds the
digits 1 to 5 as names, so `gog_table()` needs its `text` argument for this
table ([Labels that look like
numbers](../book-data.qmd#labels-that-look-like-numbers) shows it in all four
languages):

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(storm_seasons)
```

Three categorical columns need three places. The column with the most
different values goes on an axis, and the one with the fewest goes into panels.
`month` has twelve values, `category` five and `hemisphere` two. The months
repeat every year, so `polar()` puts them around a circle, with December next
to January. `stack` puts the five categories of each month into one wedge, with
category 1 at the center. This is a stacked **rose** ([Polar](../polar.qmd)):

```{r}
data(storm_seasons) + bar * stack + x(month) + y(storms) + color(category) +
  palette(c("gold", "yellowgreen", "lightseagreen", "royalblue", "indigo")) +
  polar() | facet(hemisphere)
```

*"Given the storm seasons: bars derived by stack, x is month, y is storms, color
by category, with a palette of gold, yellowgreen, lightseagreen, royalblue and
indigo, in polar, split into panel columns by hemisphere."*

The two seasons fall in opposite halves of the year. In the Northern Hemisphere
most storms begin from June to November, and September has the most, 378. In
the Southern Hemisphere most begin from December to April, February has the
most, 142, and no storm began in July or August. [Play](../play.qmd) counted
477 storms for September in the north, because there a storm is counted in
every month it lasts. The north has more than twice as many storms, 1,560
against 614. The colors run from light for category 1 to dark for category 5,
and the strongest storms are the dark outer end of each wedge. Over the whole
year, category 4 storms outnumber category 2 and category 3 storms in both
hemispheres.

You can also put the category on an axis and show each count as the shade of a
tile. gog puts the first category at the top of a `y` axis.
`order(category, desc = TRUE)` runs the axis the other way, so category 1 is at
the bottom, as in the [population
pyramid](groups.qmd#where-does-a-population-pyramid-come-from):

```{r}
data(storm_seasons) + zone + x(month) + y(category) + color(storms) +
  order(category, desc = TRUE) | facet(hemisphere)
```

*"Given the storm seasons: zones, x is month, y is category, color by storms,
ordered by category, largest first, split into panel columns by hemisphere."*

Each tile is one count, and an empty cell is a month and category with no
storm. The three darkest tiles are all in the north: category 1 in August and
September, 116 and 111, and category 4 in September, 103. A shade is harder to
compare than a length. So the rose shows the shape of each season more clearly,
and the tiles give each count its own place, by month and category.

Two other charts are made for tables of categories. A
[mosaic](../transforms.qmd#the-mosaic) gives each combination an area as large
as its count. An [alluvial diagram](../flow.qmd) makes each column a stage, and
carries each count from one stage to the next in a band.

## Which categories are alike?

The storm tiles had an order on both axes, months and categories. The
`nutrients` table has none. It gives the amount of five nutrients in each of
eight foods. The question is which foods resemble each other, and which
nutrients are found in the same foods. As with the storms, the amount goes on
`color` in a tile plot. The slot order on each axis is the order the rows arrived in,
and that order carries no meaning. So here the amount also sets the order of
both axes. Build a [cluster](../cluster.qmd) tree on each axis, then compose the
three plots: the tree above, the tiles below it, and the second tree on the
right. `theme(legend = "bottom")` puts the tile plot's legend under the tiles,
so the tree on the right stands next to them. Each shared axis takes its leaf
order from the tree along that side.
Tiles of similar color then sit next to each other.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(nutrients)
```

```{r}
(data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + x(food) +
   theme(height = 150)) /
  ((data(nutrients) + zone + x(food) + y(nutrient) + color(amount) +
      theme(legend = "bottom")) |
     (data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = food) + y(nutrient) +
        theme(width = 150)))
```

*"Given nutrients: paths derived by cluster on amount, over nutrient, x is food;
above zones, x is food, y is nutrient, color by amount, beside paths derived by
cluster on amount, over food, y is nutrient."*

Chicken and salmon sit side by side, both dark on protein, and oats, rice,
beans and lentils sit together, dark on carbs. Almonds join the top tree last,
and their fat tile is the darkest on the page. In the tree on the right, iron
and fiber join first: their amounts are the most alike across the eight foods.
Owning chapters: [Cluster](../cluster.qmd), [Zone](../marks/zone.qmd).

## What this section refuses

An earlier recipe put population on `size`, and `shape` may look like a channel
that could carry it too. The seven glyphs have no order from smallest to
largest, so `shape` refuses a continuous column and names channels that do carry
magnitude:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + shape(population)
```
